bib.title: MCP Server Architecture Patterns for LLM-Integrated Applications

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "MCP Server Architecture Patterns for LLM-Integrated Applications", Carson Rodrigues (Celabe, operator of the ANSYR voice AI platform) and Oysturn Vas (University of Waterloo). arXiv:2606.30317v1 [cs.SE], 29 Jun 2026. The text says it is an ICSME Industry Track "industry experience paper". It is a preprint as far as the file shows. Conflict of interest, disclosed in the text: the first author's employer supplies the production corpus and the tool-count data.

COVERAGE: All 9 pages, 44,962 of 44,962 chars read, including the limitations, threats to validity, AI disclosure and reference tail. The only part I skimmed was the reference list. Extraction was clean. I did not pull the figures with the figures script. Fig 1 and Fig 2 captions came from the text. The page numbers below are my estimates, because the extraction has no page markers. Offsets are line numbers in the extracted text file (/Users/ramsey-wise/.claude/projects/-Users-ramsey-wise-workspace-learn-ai-engineering/d3341309-9d8e-4c3c-af1e-67e453353cc0/tool-results/bbuvbtznx.txt).

VERDICT: On topic for tool descriptions and tool count in notes/10, and mostly off topic for notes/09 (protocols). The paper is a mixed design-pattern catalogue. Its one real measurement for context engineering is the tool-count study in §VI-C. That study is observational data from one company and was not run as a controlled experiment. The patterns themselves are qualitative. Treat the paper as moderate-to-weak evidence on its own, and cite its tool-count result only as a corroborating data point alongside RAG-MCP and LongFuncEval. For notes/09 the paper has only a short MCP primer, the stdio vs streamable-http latency comparison, and the LSP analogy.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Tool-selection accuracy falls below 90% between 10 and 15 tools for Haiku and at 30 tools for Sonnet.
 number: Haiku 91% at 10 tools, 87% at 15. Sonnet stays at or above 90% up to 20 tools and drops below at 30.
 setup: Retrospective analysis of ANSYR voice-AI production telemetry, Q1 2025. Buckets were 1, 3, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30 and 50 tools, with N=200 session turns per bucket. Models were Claude Haiku 4.5 and Claude Sonnet 4, assigned by tenant config. Ground truth was the tool a human operator confirmed in post-call quality review. Wilson 95% CI within ±4 points.
 quote: "Haiku drops below the 90% accuracy threshold between 10 and 15 tools (91% at 10 tools, 87% at 15); Sonnet maintains ≥90% up to 20 tools and drops below at 30 tools."
 where: §VI-C, p.5-6, lines 667-669.
 Inconsistency to flag: the abstract says Sonnet drops "between 20 and 30 tools". The body says Sonnet is at or above 90% at 20 and below at 30. These agree. Sonnet's accuracy at 30 tools is not given as a number in the text, only in Fig 2.
2. At 10 tools, Haiku is faster but less accurate than Sonnet.
 number: Haiku 91% at 245 ms median. Sonnet 95% at 410 ms.
 setup: Same telemetry as claim 1. The wall-clock figure is for a latency-constrained voice deployment.
 quote: "At 10 tools, Haiku achieves 91% accuracy at a median 245 ms; Sonnet achieves 95% at 410 ms."
 where: §VI-C, line 670-671.
3. The authors' recommended budget is about 10-15 tools per context. Past that, partition the tool set with a scoped Proxy Aggregator (per-request retrieval over tools). Static merging of many servers' tools makes it worse.
 number: ≈10-15 tools
 setup: A design recommendation derived from claim 1, not tested separately. No experiment compares scoped and static aggregation. The conclusion lists "quantitative evaluation of LLM tool selection accuracy across pattern variants" as future work.
 quote: "Plain static merging would make the problem worse rather than better, so the mitigation is selective exposure, not aggregation by itself."
 where: §VI-C, lines 672-679. See also §IV-D, lines 391-402.
4. Corroboration from other work, cited and not re-measured: RAG-MCP (Gan and Sun) and LongFuncEval (Kate et al.).
 number: >90% success only up to ≈30 candidate tools, sharp degradation beyond ≈100; a 7-85% accuracy drop as the catalog grows.
 setup: Secondhand claims from refs [20] and [23], not read by this paper's authors in a way we can check.
 quote: "Gan and Sun [20] report tool-selection success above 90% only up to ≈30 candidate tools, degrading sharply beyond ≈100, and Kate et al. [23] measure a 7–85% accuracy drop as the tool catalog grows."
 where: §VI-C, lines 681-684. Cite the originals, not this paper, for these numbers.
5. Tool descriptions are what LLMs select on. Missing or vague descriptions are an anti-pattern ("Missing or Vague Tool Descriptions"), and the paper advises writing "what the tool does, when to use it, and what it returns".
 number: none. The claim is qualitative, with no ablation of description quality.
 quote: "LLMs choose tools by reading descriptions, not by inspecting schemas. Write descriptions that explain what the tool does, when to use it, and what it returns, as if explaining it to someone who has never seen it before."
 where: §V-D, lines 494-497. See also §VIII-B, lines 729-736: "Precise, information-dense descriptions are necessary, not optional".
6. The "God Tool" is an anti-pattern: a single tool with an undifferentiated schema, such as do_anything(action, params).
 number: none. The text says accuracy "collapses" but gives no figure.
 quote: "Tool selection accuracy collapses. The fix is decomposition: give each distinct operation its own named tool with a precise schema and description."
 where: §V-A, lines 475-477. The tool-count study is in tension with this advice. Decomposing into many tools pushes the count up, while the Tool Orchestrator pattern (composite tools) pushes it down. The paper does not reconcile the two.
7. Transport overhead is dominated by network RTT, not by protocol encoding.
 number: stdio p50 0.01 ms; streamable-http loopback p50 0.39 ms, p95 0.45 ms, p99 0.48 ms. The modeled remote rows are 30.4 ms p50 for same-region remote, 38.4 ms for a remote Stateful Session Server, and 62.4 ms for a remote Proxy Aggregator with a single hop.
 setup: The measured rows are a minimal JSON-RPC echo server, N=100 calls plus 10 warm-up, loopback only, with no LLM in the loop. The three remote rows are modeled as loopback overhead plus an assumed RTT constant (≈30/80/180 ms p50/p95/p99), not measured. Do not cite the 38.4 ms and 62.4 ms rows as measurements.
 quote: "The substantive finding: transport overhead is dominated by network RTT, not by the protocol layer."
 where: §VI-B and Table III, lines 552-597.
8. Five MCP server patterns can be applied consistently by two LLM raters.
 number: Cohen's κ=0.76 (95% CI [0.62, 0.88]), 81.5% raw agreement. Agreement with the authors' labels was 68.5% (Haiku) and 75.9% (Sonnet).
 setup: 54 held-out servers, architecture-neutral descriptions written by the authors. Both raters are Claude models at temperature 0. A pilot on descriptions that name their own architecture scored 97%.
 quote: "agreement with the intended label is 69–76% once descriptions are architecture-neutral"
 where: §VI-A, lines 527-545.
 Relevance: marginal for context engineering. The result shows that statefulness and domain logic cannot be seen from a tool list.
9. The paper's own corpus is small and the patterns are descriptive. The five patterns are Resource Gateway, Tool Orchestrator, Stateful Session Server, Proxy Aggregator and Domain-Specific Adapter.
 number: 15 servers, of which 5 are the authors' own production servers and 10 are public.
 setup: Single-coder open coding with a second-author review. A candidate pattern needed to appear in at least two servers.
 quote: "We do not claim the structural skeletons are new; each has a clear ancestor in classical software architecture (Table I)."
 where: §II-B, lines 132-134, and §III.
10. Resource content must be sanitized before it reaches the model, because injected instructions in documents get treated as instructions. This is an anti-pattern and a design pattern at once, with no experiment behind it.
 quote: "A document containing "Ignore previous instructions and…" will be processed by the LLM as instruction, not data."
 where: §V-B, lines 481-482.
11. Long-running tools should return a job ID and expose a poll tool.
 quote: "MCP has no built-in async callback mechanism; the client times out."
 where: §V-C, lines 487-490. This claim is dated: later MCP spec revisions may have changed it.
12. Smaller items for notes/09: MCP is built on JSON-RPC 2.0 with three primitives (tools, resources, prompts) and two transports (stdio and streamable-http). The paper compares MCP to the Language Server Protocol. It recommends authenticating at the transport layer, returning structured errors so the model can retry, and logging tool name, input hash, latency, output size and error code per call (§II-A, §VII).

LIMITS
- The tool-count data is retrospective production telemetry from one voice-AI deployment. The paper states: "the data is observational and from one organization's production tool surface; results may differ for tool inventories that emphasize semantically overlapping tools or tools with deliberately vague descriptions".
- The raw logs are not released: "the figures cannot be re-derived purely from the released code". Only a CSV of per-bucket numbers is released, and I could not check it.
- Tool descriptions are never varied in any experiment, so the claim that description quality drives selection is argued, not measured.
- The paper does not control for tool overlap, description length, or token cost of the tool schemas. It also does not report how many tokens the schemas consume.
- Only two Claude models (Haiku 4.5 and Sonnet 4) were tested. No other families and no later models, so the thresholds have likely dated.
- The authors concede: single-coder derivation of the taxonomy, a corpus from one organisation, a 54-server reliability set judged by LLMs that may share blind spots, three of the five latency rows modeled rather than measured, and a classification corpus of descriptions rather than running servers.
- The paper's own future-work list says no study yet links pattern choice to measured accuracy.

BUILDS ON
- Gamma et al. (Design Patterns) for the pattern format; Fowler's enterprise application patterns; Hohpe and Woolf's integration patterns [4].
- Saldaña, The Coding Manual for Qualitative Researchers, 4th ed., 2021, for the coding method.
- Gan and Sun, "RAG-MCP: Mitigating prompt bloat in LLM tool selection via retrieval-augmented generation", arXiv:2505.03275, 2025, for retrieval-over-tools.
- Kate, Pedapati, Basu et al., "LongFuncEval", arXiv:2505.10570, 2025.
- Guo et al., "A measurement study of model context protocol ecosystem", arXiv:2509.25292, 2025, which counts more than 8,000 servers.
- Hasan et al. [17] on maintainability smells in MCP servers, and Hou et al. [16] on MCP security.
- Anthropic's MCP specification, November 2024.
- ReAct [12], LSP [7], and OpenAI/Anthropic function-calling docs [5][6].

CODE: Listing 4, the namespaced routing core of the Proxy Aggregator (§IV-D, lines 403-425). Snippet: name: `${s.namespace}__${t.name}`, // e.g. "github__create_pr" ... const [ns, ...rest] = req.params.name.split('__'). It is the only snippet worth keeping, and it is a static-merge sketch with no scoped filter.

FIGURES
- Fig 2, p.5: two panels, "Accuracy vs. Tool Count" (Haiku 4.5 and Sonnet 4, with a 90% line and a shaded region at ≤10 tools) and "Latency vs. Tool Count" (a 500 ms budget line). Caption: "Tool count vs. accuracy and latency (Claude Haiku 4.5 and Claude Sonnet 4; Nb = 200 requests per bucket from ANSYR production logs)". It is the only place Sonnet's accuracy at 30 and 50 tools is shown, and I did not view it. Its y-axis range suggests accuracy sits between 60 and 100%, which I did not read exactly.
- Fig 1, p.5: transport latency bars on a log scale, with measured and modeled rows labelled. Table III has the same numbers.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions in the PDF text.
- Two harmless oddities: the first tool call returned a block of unrelated MCP server instructions (Claude Docs, Dropbox) after the output. They did not come from the PDF and I ignored them.
- Extraction has no page markers, so page numbers are estimates.
- I did not run the figures script, so I did not look at the plots.
- The abstract's "20 and 30 tools" for Sonnet matches the body, but the body does not state Sonnet's exact accuracy at 30 tools.
- Hedging note: Haiku's 91% at 10 tools is only 1 point above the 90% line, and the CI is ±4 points, so "drops below 90% between 10 and 15" is not statistically firm.
